title: Blockchain for supply chain transparency
summary: A shared ledger that lets shippers, ports and buyers track goods and paperwork end to end.
keywords: blockchain, distributed ledger, logistics, shipping, traceability, provenance, trade finance
whyTempting: Global trade really does run on scattered paperwork, and nobody trusts anyone else's database. A ledger that every party can see and nobody controls sounds like the perfect fix, and large companies were eager to announce pilots.
whyItFails:
The hard part of supply chain tracking is getting accurate data in at each step, which a ledger doesn't solve: if someone records the wrong thing, the blockchain faithfully stores the wrong thing.

The network is only valuable if competitors all join, but each one is wary of a platform run by, or benefiting, a rival. Once governance is sorted out, a conventional shared database usually does the job more cheaply.
whatWouldChange:
A new attempt needs a neutral operator that rivals are willing to trust, or a regulation that requires them to share the same data.

It should also solve the data entry problem directly, for example with sensors or automatic document capture, and be honest about whether a blockchain is needed at all.

attempts.notes: Trade finance network for banks and their corporate clients.
Built by IBM and Maersk. Struggled to get the wider shipping industry to join.

reasons.detail: Competitors wouldn't join a network that a rival controlled or benefited from.
A ledger can't verify that what was recorded matches reality.
Without broad adoption, members couldn't justify the fees.
